html:
The Guenoa and Minuane were Indigenous peoples of the grasslands of today's Uruguay and southern Brazil, between the Uruguay River and the Atlantic. Their language is thought to have been related to that of the Charrúa, and Spanish records often name them together.

They were hunters and gatherers of the open plains. After the Spanish and Portuguese brought cattle and horses, they became mounted herders and raiders, trading with both empires and sometimes with the Jesuit missions of the Guarani. In the 1700s and early 1800s colonial and then Uruguayan armies attacked them. By the time of the massacre of the Charrúa at Salsipuedes in 1831, the Guenoa and Minuane had largely merged into other groups or the rural population.
